claims.text: A blockchain is an append-only chain of blocks where each block stores the hash of the previous block, so altering an earlier transaction requires rewriting that block and every block after it; copies are spread across many independent nodes that agree without a central administrator.
Value moves from transaction to transaction: a transaction's inputs spend the outputs of earlier transactions, and an output may be spent only once — a second spend is rejected as a double spend.

A key pair uses 256-bit private keys: a private key signs and derives a public key, and the common P2PKH form pays to the hash of the public key, encoded for sharing as a base58check address with a checksum.
Decentralization matters to an app builder because there is no central server to run or secure, no single point of failure, no single company to shut the app down, and no hosted backend to depend on.

uncertainties.resolution: The manifest fixes the phrasing as 'about a second'; the lesson states that effect and never names the InstantSend-vs-ChainLock locking mechanics, which are mustNotCover.

uncertainties.topic: Why decentralization matters to a builder is a pedagogical inference
uncertainties.resolution: The lesson leads with concrete build-time benefits (no server to run or secure, no single point of failure, nobody can shut it down, no hosted backend), grounded in the docs' decentralized language.

mustCover concepts (blockchain, transaction, keys, address, masternode) are taught in prose. Incidental jargon reuses existing ids (block, node, duff, fiat, premine, ico, evonode, dapi); 'node' and 'mining' were appended, and no mustNotCover term was smuggled in.

uncertainties.topic: Describing 'one network, two jobs' without crossing the mustNotCover boundary
uncertainties.resolution: Dash Platform is described only as the application-data layer via Drive (storage) and DAPI (the read/write API), with no mention of identities, data contracts, documents, LLMQs, quorums, or Tenderdash.
